name: Tyconius
knownFor: Donatist writer of Africa whose Book of Rules gave seven keys for reading Scripture, and who argued against his own party without leaving it.
dates: Late fourth century; Gennadius of Marseilles says he flourished under Theodosius and his sons, and F. C. Burkitt reckons he wrote before 383

keyWorks.title: The Book of Rules (Liber Regularum)
keyWorks.about: seven rules for reading Scripture, from the Lord and his body to the devil and his body

keyWorks.title: Commentary on the Apocalypse
keyWorks.about: the whole book read in a spiritual sense; believed lost, though later writers took much of it into their own

keyWorks.title: On Internal War
keyWorks.about: on the quarrels within the church, named by Gennadius; Burkitt says it has perished

traces: Augustine of Hippo set out all seven rules in On Christian Doctrine, Book 3, and commended the book to students.
F. C. Burkitt names Primasius, Bede and above all Beatus, a Spanish priest of Charlemagne's time, as writers who used his Apocalypse commentary as their main authority.
remembered: Augustine calls him one "who, although a Donatist himself, has written most triumphantly against the Donatists."
Gennadius says he was, "it is said, sufficiently learned in sacred literature, not wholly unacquainted with secular literature and zealous in ecclesiastical affairs."
Burkitt says that throughout his review Augustine "treats Tyconius as an authority to be explained rather than as a theorist to be criticised."

uncertain: Burkitt says the little known of his life comes chiefly from Augustine of Hippo, who was his critic and also drew on his book. Augustine calls him a Donatist who wrote against the Donatists, and "of a most inconsistent disposition" for staying with them.

What Tyconius reported about a Donatist council of two hundred and seventy bishops reaches us through Augustine's Letter 93. Augustine says Parmenian checked him by his reply but did not refute the facts, and that Tyconius said many were still living who could prove them.
Augustine faults his teaching that faith is our own and does not come from God. He adds that Tyconius wrote before the Pelagian quarrel, "having no enemy to guard against" on this point.
Burkitt's date before 383 rests on his reading of one passage, and he hedges it: "it would seem that Tyconius wrote before 383 AD."
The sources used here do not give his birth, death, home town or whether he was ordained. A Donatist council's condemnation of him around 380 is not found in the sources used here.
